guides.title: Best AI coding tool for beginners (2026)
guides.metaTitle: Best AI Coding Tool for Beginners (2026): Honest Picks – ShipRank
guides.desc: The best AI coding tools for beginners in 2026: GitHub Copilot, Replit, Cursor, Devin Desktop and Claude Code compared on free plans, price and learning curve.
guides.intro: If you want to learn to code, or at least understand the code AI writes for you, you need a different tool from a no-code app builder. These are the AI coding tools we'd hand a beginner in October 2026, ranked by how gentle the learning curve is and how far the free plan gets you.

top.html:
Start with GitHub Copilot's free plan inside VS Code if you're following a course or tutorial. If you don't want to install anything, use Replit in your browser. Once you're building real projects and want a stronger agent, move up to Cursor. Save Claude Code for when you're comfortable in a terminal.

Don't want to write code at all? You'll be happier with a prompt-to-app builder. See our best AI app builders for beginners guide instead.

notes.GitHub Copilot: The free plan includes 2,000 code completions a month plus limited chat and agent use, and it runs inside VS Code, the editor most tutorials use. Pro is $10/month.
notes.Replit: There's nothing to install: you write, run and host code in the browser, and Free Mode lets you start without paying. The Core plan is $20/month ($18 billed annually).
notes.Cursor: The most popular AI editor and our #1 overall. The free plan has limited agent and chat requests. Plus ($8/month) only includes Grok models, and Premium ($30/month) adds cloud agents and other providers' models at API list price.
notes.Windsurf: Windsurf is now called Devin Desktop, and its plans carried over unchanged. It's built around running several agents at once, which is more than most beginners need.
notes.Claude Code: Claude Code isn't included on Claude's Free plan. It needs Pro ($20/month, or $17/month billed annually) or above. It's a superb agent, but it's terminal-first, which is a hurdle on day one.

sections.html:
For beginners, the best AI coding tool isn't the one with the most powerful agent. It's the one that teaches you the least confusing workflow and doesn't surprise you with a bill. We weighed four things:

  • Free plan: can you learn for weeks without paying?
  • Familiar setup: does it work where tutorials and courses already are, such as VS Code or the browser?
  • Explains as well as writes: can you ask why the code works, not just get code back?
  • Predictable cost: most tools now meter usage in credits or allowances, so you need to know what happens when you run out.

Prices and plan details below come from each tool's official pricing page, checked on 27 October 2026.

• Inline suggestions and a chat panel. Seeing a suggestion as you type, then asking "explain this line", is the fastest way to learn. Copilot and Cursor both do this inside the editor.
  • An agent that asks before acting. Agents can edit many files and run commands. Claude Code, for example, asks permission before changing files or running commands. Keep those prompts switched on while you're learning.
  • Usage you can see. Copilot shows usage and alerts at 75%, 90% and 100% of any budget you set. Cursor's allowance refreshes weekly, so one heavy day doesn't wipe out your month.
  • Somewhere to run your code. Replit runs and hosts in the browser. With an editor like Cursor or Copilot you run code on your own computer and deploy with a host such as Vercel or Netlify.

sections.h: A simple path from beginner to shipping
sections.html:
1. Week 1–2: install VS Code and turn on GitHub Copilot Free. Follow any beginner course and use chat to explain every suggestion you accept.
  2. Week 3–4: build one small project end to end, such as a to-do list or a personal site. If setup is fighting you, build it on Replit instead.
  3. Month 2: try Cursor's free plan and use the agent for multi-file changes. Read every change before you accept it.
  4. When you're comfortable in a terminal: try a coding agent like Claude Code on a real repo. Our Cursor vs Claude Code guide explains when each fits.

Want to compare the editors side by side? See Cursor vs Windsurf vs GitHub Copilot and our best AI code editors ranking.

• Accepting code you can't explain. If you can't say what a block does, ask the AI to explain it before moving on. That habit is what turns AI help into actual learning.
  • Pasting secrets into prompts or code. Keep API keys in environment variables, never in files you push to GitHub.
  • Vague prompts. "Make it better" burns credits. "Add a delete button to each to-do item and save the list to localStorage" gets results.
  • Skipping git. Commit before every big AI change so you can undo it. Agents occasionally go in the wrong direction.
  • Paying too early. Every tool here except Claude Code has a free plan. Upgrade when you hit the limit regularly, not before.

faq: What is the best AI coding tool for complete beginners?

GitHub Copilot's free plan in VS Code is the easiest place to start if you're learning from tutorials. Replit is the easiest if you don't want to install anything. If you don't want to write code at all, use an app builder like Lovable or Bolt.new instead.
Is GitHub Copilot free?
Yes. Copilot Free includes 2,000 code completions a month and limited chat and agent usage. Copilot Pro is $10/month (checked 27 Oct 2026).
Is Cursor free?
Yes, Cursor has a free plan with limited agent and chat requests. Paid plans start at $8/month (Plus, Grok models only), and Premium is $30/month (checked 27 Oct 2026).
Is Claude Code free?

No. Claude Code isn't included on Claude's Free plan. It comes with Claude Pro ($20/month, or $17/month billed annually) and higher plans, or you can pay per use with API credits through a Claude Console account.
Will using AI stop me from learning to code?

It can if you accept code blindly. Used well, it speeds learning up: ask the AI to explain each suggestion, try writing small pieces yourself first, and use the agent for boring setup rather than for the concepts you're trying to learn.
What happened to Windsurf?
Windsurf has been renamed Devin Desktop by Cognition. According to Devin's FAQ, existing plans, pricing, extensions and settings carry over automatically, and the Pro plan is $20/month.

guides.title: Best AI tool to build a website without code (2026)
guides.metaTitle: Best AI Tool to Build a Website Without Code (2026) – ShipRank
guides.desc: Build a website without code using AI. Lovable, Bolt.new, v0, Replit, Builder.io and Figma Make compared on free plans, hosting and custom domains.
guides.intro: You can now describe a website in plain English and get a working, hosted site back, no code required. The catch is in the details: free plans, branding, custom domains and what happens when you run out of credits. Here's how the main AI website and app builders compare in October 2026.

top.html: Lovable is the best all-round choice if you've never coded and want a site that can grow into an app with logins and a database. Bolt.new is the quickest way to a hosted site for free, but free sites carry Bolt branding. v0 suits you if you'd like clean React/Next.js code on Vercel. If you already have a design in Figma, use Builder.io (affiliate link) or Figma Make.

guides.picksTitle: The best AI website builders, ranked

notes.Lovable: The free plan gives 5 build credits a day (up to 30 a month) plus 20 Cloud credits a month for hosting. Lovable's FAQ says you own the code and projects you build.
notes.Bolt.new: The free plan includes website hosting and 1M tokens a month (300K a day), but sites show Bolt branding. Your own domain and no branding need Pro at $25/month.
notes.v0: The free plan allows 7 messages a day and deploys to Vercel. It has a visual Design Mode and GitHub sync. The output is React/Next.js, so it's the most developer-friendly option here.
notes.Replit: Build and host in one place with an agent. Core is $20/month ($18 billed annually). It's better for apps than for simple brochure sites.
notes.Builder.io: Best when you already have a Figma design. The free plan includes the Figma plugin and 15 credits a day (60 a month max). Custom domains need Pro at $24/user/month.
notes.Figma Make: Best for designers already working in Figma. Make is included with a Professional Full seat ($16/month). The $12 Dev seat doesn't include it.

sections.html:
• Portfolio, landing page or small business site: Bolt.new or Lovable. Both go from prompt to live site in minutes. Budget for a paid plan if you want your own domain without branding on Bolt.
  • A site with sign-ups, logins or a database: Lovable, which pairs with Supabase, or Replit. See our Supabase vs Firebase comparison for the backend.
  • A marketing site from an existing design: Builder.io (affiliate link) or Figma Make. Read our Figma to code guide for the workflow.
  • You might hire a developer later: v0, because its React/Next.js output and GitHub sync are what most web developers already use.

For a deeper head-to-head, see Lovable vs Bolt.new vs v0 vs Replit and our best AI app builders ranking.

sections.h: Custom domains, hosting and hidden costs
sections.html:
Almost every builder lets you start free. The differences show up when you go live:

  • Branding: Bolt.new's free plan adds Bolt branding to sites. Removing it, along with adding your own domain, is part of Pro ($25/month).
  • Custom domains: Builder.io lists custom domains on Pro ($24/user/month), not on Free.
  • Hosting costs: Lovable says hosting for most small or new apps is covered by the Cloud grant included with plans. Busy sites can start using credits.
  • Credits expire: Lovable's unused monthly credits expire two months after they're issued, and its daily free credits don't roll over. Bolt's Pro tokens do roll over.
  • Hosting it yourself: if your builder lets you export code or sync to GitHub (v0 and Builder.io both connect to GitHub), you can host on the free tiers of Vercel or Netlify. See Vercel vs Netlify.

sections.h: How to build your first site in an afternoon
sections.html:
1. Write a one-paragraph brief before you open any tool: who the site is for, the pages you need, the one action visitors should take, and two or three sites whose style you like.
  2. Paste the brief as your first prompt. Ask for the page structure first, then the design. Smaller, specific prompts use fewer credits than "redo everything".
  3. Fix one thing per prompt. For example, "Make the hero headline shorter and the button green". Lovable's own examples show small edits like this costing about half a credit.
  4. Check mobile. Open the preview on your phone before publishing.
  5. Set page titles and descriptions for each page so search engines know what it's about.
  6. Publish, then connect a domain when you're happy, upgrading only if your tool requires it.

sections.h: When a no-code AI builder is the wrong choice
sections.html: AI builders are excellent for getting something live fast. They're less suited to large content sites with hundreds of pages, complex custom logic, or teams that need tight control over every line of code. If that's you, learn the basics with an AI code editor. Start with our best AI coding tool for beginners guide.

faq: Can I really build a website without any code?

Yes. Lovable, Bolt.new, v0 and Replit all turn plain-English prompts into working sites, and Lovable and Bolt.new include hosting. You'll still need to review the result, write your own content and check it on mobile.
What is the best free AI website builder?

For a completely free live site, Bolt.new includes hosting on its free plan (with Bolt branding), and Lovable's free plan includes daily build credits plus monthly Cloud hosting credits. v0's free plan deploys to Vercel with a limit of 7 messages a day.
Can I use my own domain for free?

Usually not on the builder itself. Bolt.new and Builder.io put custom domains on paid plans. If you export the code to GitHub, you can host it on Vercel's or Netlify's free tier and connect a domain you own there.
Do I own the website I build with AI?
Lovable's pricing FAQ states that you own the code, projects and AI output you create. Check each tool's terms, and keep a copy of your code on GitHub where the tool allows it.
Is an AI-built website good for SEO?

It can be, as long as each page has a clear title, a meta description, real content and fast loading. Bolt.new's Pro plan lists an "SEO boost" for published sites. Whatever you use, write the words yourself rather than leaving placeholder AI text.

guides.title: Cursor vs Claude Code (2026): which should you use?
guides.metaTitle: Cursor vs Claude Code (2026): Which Should You Use? – ShipRank
guides.desc: Cursor vs Claude Code for vibe coders: AI editor vs terminal-first agent, models, free plans and pricing compared from official pages, with an honest verdict.
guides.intro: Cursor and Claude Code are two of the most popular ways to build with AI, but they're different kinds of tool. Cursor is an AI code editor with agents built in. Claude Code is Anthropic's coding agent, which you steer from the terminal, your editor, the web or Slack. Here's how to choose, with pricing checked on 27 October 2026.

top.html: Pick Cursor if you want to see and edit code in a visual editor, switch between models from different providers, and start on a free plan. Pick Claude Code if you're comfortable in a terminal and want to hand off bigger, longer-running tasks like refactors, migrations or "fix this issue and open a pull request". Many builders use both: Claude Code has a native extension that runs inside Cursor.

notes.Cursor: A VS Code-style editor with agents, plus a CLI, Slack integration and AI pull request reviews on GitHub. Free plan available. Plus is $8/month (Grok models only), Premium is $30/month.
notes.Claude Code: Runs in the terminal, with extensions for VS Code, Cursor, Devin Desktop and JetBrains, plus web, desktop, mobile and Slack. Not on Claude's Free plan; Pro is $20/month ($17/month billed annually).

sections.h: The core difference: editor vs agent
sections.html:
Cursor is where you write code. You get tab completions, inline edits and a chat panel. Its agent can plan and make multi-file changes, and on higher plans you can launch cloud agents that work in parallel. You stay close to the code and review diffs as they happen.

Claude Code is a coding agent you direct. Anthropic describes it as handling everything from bug fixes and tests to multi-hour refactors. It explores the codebase on its own, runs your tests and can open pull requests through GitHub and GitLab. Used in the terminal, it runs locally and asks permission before changing files or running commands.

In practice, Cursor feels like pair programming and Claude Code feels like delegating to a colleague.

One thing to know about Cursor in 2026: its plans are now bundled with an X/Grok subscription. Plus only includes Grok models. Premium and above include Grok usage, and other providers' models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) are billed separately at API list price.

Cursor is model-agnostic. Its model picker includes options from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI and Cursor's own models, so you can pick a cheap fast model for small edits and a frontier model for hard problems. Claude Code uses Anthropic's Claude models. On the Pro plan, Claude's pricing page lists Opus, Sonnet and Haiku.

Choose Cursor if you:

  • Are newer to coding and want to see every change in a visual editor
  • Want a free plan to start
  • Like switching between models from different providers
  • Want completions while you type, not just an agent

Choose Claude Code if you:

  • Are comfortable with the terminal and git
  • Want to delegate larger tasks and review the results
  • Already pay for Claude Pro or Max for chat, since Claude Code is included
  • Work across big, unfamiliar codebases

Still deciding? Compare more options in Cursor vs Windsurf vs GitHub Copilot, Claude Code vs OpenAI Codex vs Devin, and our rankings of the best AI code editors and best coding agents.

Yes, and it's a common setup. Anthropic lists native Claude Code extensions for VS Code, Cursor and Devin Desktop. You can edit and review in Cursor while Claude Code handles a bigger task in the terminal. The trade-off is cost: you'd be paying for two subscriptions, so start with one and add the other only if you hit its limits.

faq: Is Cursor better than Claude Code?

Neither is better at everything. Cursor is better if you want a visual editor, a free plan and a choice of models. Claude Code is better for delegating large, multi-step tasks from the terminal. ShipRank ranks Cursor #1 among AI code editors and Claude Code #1 among coding agents.
Is Claude Code free?

No. Claude Code isn't included on Claude's Free plan. It comes with Pro ($20/month, or $17/month billed annually), Max (from $100/month), Team and Enterprise plans, or pay-as-you-go API usage through a Claude Console account.
How much does Cursor cost in 2026?

Cursor has a free plan. Paid plans are Plus at $8/month (Grok models only), Premium at $30/month, Super at $100/month and Ultra at $200/month. Third-party models are billed separately at API list price (checked 27 Oct 2026).
Can I use Claude models in Cursor?

Yes. Cursor's model picker includes Anthropic models, but on Premium and above they're billed separately at API list price rather than drawing from your plan's included usage. The Plus plan only includes Grok models.
Can I run Claude Code inside Cursor?
Yes. Anthropic offers a native Claude Code extension that works in VS Code, Cursor and Devin Desktop, and you can also run it in Cursor's built-in terminal.

guides.title: How to turn Figma designs into code with AI (2026)
guides.metaTitle: Figma to Code with AI (2026): Best Tools and Step-by-Step – ShipRank
guides.desc: Turn Figma designs into React, HTML or full apps with AI: Figma Make, Builder.io Visual Copilot, Lovable and v0 compared, with prices and a step-by-step guide.
guides.intro: Hand-coding a Figma design used to take days. AI design-to-code tools now get you most of the way in minutes, but they solve two different problems. Some turn a design into a clickable prototype, and others turn it into production code in your real codebase. Here's which tool to use for each, and how to get clean output.

top.html: For a fast, interactive prototype without leaving Figma, use Figma Make. For production code that uses your own components and framework, use Builder.io (affiliate link)'s Visual Copilot. If you want a full-stack app with a database from your design, Builder.io's Figma-to-Lovable route or Lovable on its own is the no-code path.

notes.Figma Make: Lives inside Figma. Everything it builds is code-backed and visually editable, and you can attach designs and use your libraries as context. Included with a Professional Full seat ($16/month). Building on your local codebase is in beta, listed as "coming soon".
notes.Builder.io: Its Visual Copilot outputs React, Angular, Vue, Svelte, Qwik, HTML/CSS and Tailwind, plus SwiftUI, React Native, Flutter and Kotlin for mobile. It can map designs to your own component library. The free plan includes the Figma plugin and a VS Code extension.
notes.Lovable: A prompt-to-app builder. Builder.io offers a Figma-to-Lovable route that turns designs into full-stack apps you then keep building by chatting.
notes.v0: Outputs React/Next.js with a visual Design Mode, GitHub sync and Vercel deploys. We haven't verified a direct Figma import, so treat it as a rebuild-from-reference option.

sections.h: Two different jobs: prototype or production code
sections.html:
Before choosing a tool, decide what the output is for:

  • Prototype: you want something clickable to test with users or show a client. Code quality matters less than speed. Figma Make is built for this.
  • Production front-end: you want components your developers will merge, using your design system, framework and styling. This is Builder.io's strength, with more setup in exchange for code that fits your codebase.
  • A full app: you want the design working with logins and data. Use an app builder like Lovable, starting from the design via Builder.io or from screenshots and prompts.

See our best design-to-code tools ranking for how we rate them overall.

sections.h: Step by step: Figma to production code with Builder.io
sections.html:
1. Clean up the frame first using the tips below. Better structure gives better code.
  2. Install the Builder.io Figma plugin. It's included on the free plan, along with GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket connections.
  3. Select a frame and export it through Visual Copilot, choosing your framework (for example React) and styling (for example Tailwind CSS or CSS Modules).
  4. Map to your components. If your team has a component library, map design components to it so the output reuses your real buttons and cards instead of new markup. Pro supports up to 3 design systems and Free supports 1.
  5. Refine with prompts, then pull the code into your repo with the VS Code extension or a Git connection, and review it like any other pull request.

Builder.io's free plan gives 15 credits a day (60 a month max). Pro is $24/user/month with 500 credits, and extra credits cost $25 per 500. Try it here: Builder.io (affiliate link).

sections.h: Step by step: prototypes with Figma Make
sections.html:
1. Open Figma Make from a Figma file on a seat that includes Make (a Professional Full seat is $16/month).
  2. Attach your design and describe the behaviour you want, such as "make the tabs switch and the form validate". Plan mode lets you agree a structured plan before it builds.
  3. Use point-and-edit to click elements in the preview and restyle or re-prompt them.
  4. Share it for comments, publish it, or copy it back to the canvas as design layers to keep polishing.

sections.h: Tips for cleaner code from any Figma design
sections.html:
• Use auto layout everywhere. It maps naturally to flexbox and grid, so the code comes out responsive instead of absolutely positioned.
  • Name your layers ("PricingCard", not "Frame 427"). Names often become component and class names.
  • Use components and variants for repeated elements so the AI generates one reusable component rather than ten copies.
  • Use styles and variables for colours, type and spacing so they become tokens rather than hard-coded values.
  • Design the mobile breakpoint too, or tell the tool explicitly how the layout should collapse.
  • Treat the output as a first draft. Review accessibility, semantics and state handling before shipping.

• Figma Make: Professional Full seat $16/month with 3,000 AI credits a month. The Starter plan is free with up to 500 AI credits a month, but we couldn't confirm which Make features it includes.
  • Builder.io: Free (15 credits a day, 60 a month max). Pro is $24/user/month.
  • Lovable: the free plan gives 5 build credits a day, up to 30 a month. We couldn't see paid prices on the pricing page when we checked.
  • v0: the free plan allows 7 messages a day. Plus is $30/user/month.

Checked on official pricing pages on 27 Oct 2026. Prices in USD.

Going from design to a working app? Pair this with our best AI website builders guide and the Lovable vs Bolt vs v0 vs Replit comparison.

faq: Can AI convert Figma to code?

Yes. Tools like Builder.io's Visual Copilot convert Figma frames into React, Vue, Angular, Svelte, HTML/CSS, Tailwind and mobile frameworks, and Figma Make builds working, code-backed prototypes inside Figma. Expect to review and tidy the output before shipping it.
What is the best Figma to React tool?

For production React that reuses your own components, Builder.io's Visual Copilot is the strongest option we've reviewed, because it can map designs to your component library. For quick React prototypes inside Figma, use Figma Make.
Is Figma Make free?

Figma Make is included with a Professional Full seat ($16/month). Figma's free Starter plan includes up to 500 AI credits a month, but we couldn't confirm which Make features Starter includes. The $12 Dev seat doesn't include Make.
Is Builder.io free?
Yes. Builder.io's free plan includes the Figma plugin, a VS Code extension, Git connections and 15 AI credits a day (60 a month max). Pro is $24/user/month with 500 credits (checked 27 Oct 2026).
Do I need a clean Figma file to get good code?

It helps a lot. Builder.io says it handles structured or unstructured designs, but auto layout, named layers, components and variables consistently produce more responsive, reusable code from any tool.
